summary.en: US authorities have taken a fugitive businessman into custody in Venezuela on bribery charges while President Maduro appears in court as the United States targets his associates in a corruption scandal and a judge denied medical bail for Cilia Flores, prompting solidarity campaigns. An aid worker reports severe earthquake damage in Venezuela and Starlink internet is now permitted to operate in the country, while Cuba’s grid collapse adds regional energy strain. Energy firms are recruiting former US officials to access Venezuelan oil and allegations claim a PDVSA plane was used to transport goods. 2 battle-related deaths in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: US-myndighetene har tatt en flyktning forretningsmann i forvaring i Venezuela på bestikkelsesanklage mens president Maduro møter i retten mens USA retter seg mot hans medarbeidere i en korrupsjonsskandale, og en dommer avslo medisinsk kausjon for Cilia Flores, noe som har ført til solidaritetsk kampanjer. En hjelpearbeider rapporterer om alvorlige jordskjelvskader i Venezuela og Starlink-internett er nå tillatt å operere i landet, mens Cubas strømbrudd øker den regionale energistrømmen. Energiselskaper rekrutterer tidligere amerikanske tjenestemenn for å få tilgang til venezuelansk olje og påstander hevder at et PDVSA-fly ble brukt til å transportere varer. 2 kamprelaterte dødsfall i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
